<reason>B won by holding the burden frame and turning A's best moves against it. A's strongest cards — the equivalence-testing critique, the selection-underperformance dilemma, and the catch that B2.5's "offsetting negatives" contradict B1.5 — forced real qualifications, but B absorbed each one: whole-population registries and census-linked data answered the power objection at policy-relevant effect sizes; A's own stepfamily analogy was boomeranged into proof the instruments detect real structural effects yet find none for parental gender; and A's "recognition is doing part of the work" was flipped into the affirmative case for the policy limb. A's only affirmative mechanism (biological separation) arrived in Rebuttal 2 and dissolved in B's closing — it is shared by adoptive and donor-conceived different-sex families, is not caused by parental gender, and those children are already in the data. A's strategic concession of custody, benefits, and hospital access left CON defending only a thin residue (don't encode equivalence as settled fact), which B's "a standard no family form could satisfy is a veto on evidence" defused. A never produced an observed deficit or an opposed concrete protection, so both limbs of the motion survived. A's clipped opening cost it a never-recovered irreversibility argument.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's double jiu-jitsu in Rebuttal 2: converting A's stepfamily analogy into evidence that the research tradition catches real effects (registering none for parental gender), and converting A's "recognition does part of the work" concession into the very lever the policy limb pulls — followed by the closing dissolution of A's late biological-separation mechanism.</best_rebuttal>
